en: Preface to the Commentary on the Chapter on the Universal Door of Avalokiteśvara’s Power:
Among those who practice the single gate of the Pure Land, there are many;

yet the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation in this Chapter on the Universal Door of Śrī-Ābhāsvara is the most intimate and direct step toward the Pure Land—a wondrous remedy for curing ailments and a vast treasure for relieving poverty.
A great vessel for crossing the sea of suffering, and a rain of wondrous jewels from the many treasures;

Amitābha, the Compassionate Father, extends his golden arms through the long night and displays his jade-like rays amidst the dark alleys. At no time and in no place does he fail to welcome and guide sentient beings;

throughout many kalpas and many lifetimes, he constantly pursues and remembers the wayfarers. How could this not have been extracted by a person from within the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*? [Thus] one should participate in the practice of seated meditation.
This has been treasured within my breast for a long time. In the year of Yihai, while at the White Horse Mountain Hermitage in Yue, I casually composed this "Small Grass" (a brief work).
The metaphors within the sutras are subtle; the more I have probed and revered them, the more I find them firm and lofty.

Two or three companions wished to have it carved into printing blocks, so I entrusted it to the engravers to circulate it among the world. Those who recognize the truth may laugh, but how could I dare avoid their censure? I only pray—
If every person were like one who focuses their mindfulness, and each were like a mother remembering her child, then throughout successive lives, mother and child would never be separated;
they will certainly see the Buddha in the present and in the future.
On the first day of the intercalary month of the fifth lunar month in the eighth year of the Chongzhen era, the year being Yihai (1635), the Bhikṣu Zhengxiang, whose name is Tiri,
composed this annotated commentary on the Chapter of the Great Power Attainment of Avalokiteśvara’s Perfect Penetration.
A Commentary on the Name by the Later-Generation Bhikṣu Zhengxiang, a Disciple of the Tiantai Teachings. △ Chapter One:
The Thirteenfold Sectional Analysis. First, Explaining the Name.
The *Contemplation Sutra* states: "By means of the light of wisdom, universally illumine all sentient beings, causing them to leave the three miserable realms and attain..."
The name "Unsurpassed Power" refers to Mahāsthāmaprāpta; this is one way of receiving the name based on his transformation of others.
Furthermore, it is said that whenever he presses the earth with his toe, all the palaces of Māra and the entire trichiliocosm tremble;
this is how he receives the name Mahāsthāmaprāpta based on his power to subdue through majestic might. The Sūtra says: "I have no discrimination; I universally gather and encompass the six [senses]."
When the faculties are pure and mindfulness succeeds one another as one enters *samādhi*, this is called the "Great Power Attainment" (*Mahāsthāmaprāpta*).

This is designated as "perfect penetration" (*yuan-tong*) based on self-benefit within the causal stage; its meaning lies in universal pervasion and interpenetration. It perfectly encompasses the two virtues of the *dharmakāya* and *prajñā*.
"Penetration" means that the single path is level and uniform, such that the three periods of time do not obstruct one another—this is the virtue of liberation. Thus, it relies upon principle...

This explains "Perfect Penetration" (*yuantong*). An ordinary person of the mundane stage, by reciting the name of the Sage who has attained the ultimate fruit, finds that their body of birth-and-death immediately becomes adorned with fragrant light.
This means that the cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit, and the fruit reaches back to the source of the cause; thus, based on this practice, "Perfect Penetration" is explained.
Before interpreting this chapter, one must first clarify the fivefold profound meaning (*wuchong xuanyi*); once the profound meaning is clear, the chapter itself will be understood.
The structural framework is clearly visible: "Humanity and Dharma" is the name; the Perfectly Penetrating True Reality is the essence; Amitābha of Original Nature is the school;
the Pure and the Defiled, as well as Subduing and Gathering, are the function; and the Great Vehicle’s *maṇḍa* (fresh butter) is the teaching aspect. Regarding "Humanity and Dharma" as the name:
"Humanity" refers to the person Śrī-Ābhāsvara (Potu-shi), and "Dharma" refers to the Perfectly Penetrating Dharma. This is why it is named "Humanity and Dharma."

The intent revealed in this chapter lies in perfect penetration (*yuantong*), which constitutes its essence. When a practitioner recites the Buddha’s name, every thought-moment must directly manifest the original reality;
in every instance, one must clearly realize one's own mind. Thus, the Original Nature Amitābha is the central tenet of this chapter.
The sufferings of the Sahā world cause people to develop revulsion, while the bliss of the Pure Land causes them to give rise to joyful aspiration.

The purpose of this chapter is the application of "subduing and gathering" (zhéshè) based on such longing. Since there exists the dualistic notion of subject and object, the function of subduing and gathering belongs to the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings;
thus, the "fresh butter" (shēngsū) serves as the pedagogical characteristic (jiàoxiàng) of this chapter.
That which is called the "perfectly penetrating Pure Land" is nothing other than the one mind itself. If perfect penetration has not yet been realized, then even what is pure appears defiled.
Once Universal Pervasion (yuantong) enters, the defiled becomes pure; this precisely refers to the meaning of the "Pure Land of Mind-Only," as seen here.
Thus, the Pure Land is not a pure land external to Universal Pervasion, and Universal Pervasion is not a Universal Pervasion external to the Pure Land.
Universal Pervasion is based on the mind that creates, while the Pure Land is based on the realm that is created. This is because they are non-dual.
Duality is non-dual; if one awakens to this, then every phenomenon is revealed within one's own mind and every place manifests as the true realm.
Pure Land is not distant, and the Sahā world is not defiled. By contemplating the Buddha in this way, one attains perfect penetration everywhere.
As it is said: "If a person wishes to know the principle of true emptiness, the True Suchness within the mind pervades both the external world of sentient beings and the insentient."
They share a single essence; everywhere they are identical with the true Dharma-realm. △ Second, the formal explanation of the sutra text:
At that time, the Dharma Prince Mahāsthāmaprāpta, together with fifty-two bodhisattvas of his own rank...
This is the time when each recounted their realization of perfect penetration. The Tathāgata is the Dharma King; the Bodhisattvas are his sons who receive the consecration and assume their positions.

Those who establish the principles and bestow benevolence upon the world are the princes of the mundane realm. Those who succeed to the Buddha’s seat and continue the Buddha’s wisdom-life are the sons of the supramundane Dharma.
"Those of the same class" refers to those of the same lineage as the milk of the Dharma; they are ranked in fifty-two positions.

Regarding their number, although there were bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of ten thousand *ganges* rivers at the assembly on the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* preached by this sutra at the Jetavana Vihāra,
only fifty-two stages are enumerated because they all attained realization of perfect penetration through the same mindfulness of the Buddha.
△ Third, the respectful etiquette of the formal request:
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha.
The scribe of the sutra describes the respectful etiquette of requesting the Dharma as rising from his seat and paying homage at the Buddha’s feet; this simultaneously conveys the intended meaning.
I respectfully address the Buddha: to pay homage with the three karmas of body, speech, and mind in a state of profound devotion is the constant ritual for a disciple requesting the Dharma.
△ Fourth, clarifying the teacher: first, regarding the time, "I recall that in the past, throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River..."
I recall that in the past, when I first resolved my mind to practice, I illuminated it with the power of sovereign concentration and wisdom;
thus, there were eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. As for the Ganges, it flows from Lake Anavatapta and emerges from four mouths:
from the eastern silver-mouthed Ox Gate it issues as the Gaṅgā River, and from the southern golden-mouthed Elephant Gate...
The Sindhu River flows out from the western mouth of the Vaiḍūrya Horse; the Vakṣu River flows out from the northern mouth of the Lion;
and the Sītā River flows out from each side, circling the lake once before entering the four oceans:
the Gaṅgā enters the great southeastern ocean, the Sindhu enters the great southwestern ocean, the Vakṣu enters the great northwestern ocean, and the Sītā [enters the great northeastern ocean].
The many rivers that flow from the Lion’s Mouth into the northeastern great ocean are the source of the Yellow River in this land.
As for the frequent mention of the Ganges in the sutras, it is because the Tathāgata preached the Dharma near this river and thus used it as a metaphor.
It is forty yojanas wide and eighty yojanas long; its sand is as fine as flour, with each grain being [the size of] one *śa*.

The single gateway of "Buddha-remembrance through the visible [Buddhas]" has existed for a long time; it is also known that this represents the high rank attained by Śrī-Ābhāsvara after accumulating merit over many kalpas.
△ Second, explaining the titles of the teachers:
when a Buddha appears in the world, he is named Amitābha. Twelve Tathāgatas have succeeded one another for the duration of a kalpa, and the last of these Buddhas—
His name surpasses the light of the sun and moon; that Buddha taught me the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha.
Within kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, taking one such kalpa, twelve Tathāgatas appeared in succession.

The name of the Buddha was Immeasurable Light (*Amitābha*); his light shone radiantly upon one another without end, and for this reason he was named Immeasurable Light. Furthermore, there were twelve...
The Tathāgata is never apart from light, which has ten names: first, Immeasurable Light; second, Boundless Light;
third, Unobstructed Light; fourth, Unopposed Light; fifth, Great Flame Light; sixth, Pure Light; seventh, Joyful Light;
eighth, Wisdom Light; ninth, Uninterrupted Light; tenth, Inconceivable Light.
The first is named Unnameable Light (*Anabhihita-prabhā*), and the twelfth is named Surpassing the Sun and Moon (*Sūrya-candraprabhābhibhū*). That Buddha taught me the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*.

Regarding this, "receiving the teaching" is the beginning of establishing practice. "Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) refers to the person who is mindful; "Buddha" refers to the object contemplated by that mind;

and "samādhi" refers to the state where both subject and object are focused upon a single mind. By means of the mind one contemplates the Buddha, and by means of the Buddha one binds the mind—mind and mind [in union].
To continue in succession without interruption means that the internal mind does not arise and external objects do not invade;

one turns back to the source and returns to the fundamental unity, no longer receiving any sensations, thereby attaining *samyaksamādhi*. When this state endures without regression, one will surely reach the fruit.
Among the immeasurable samādhis, there is none that does not awaken to this; therefore, it is called the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*nienfo sanmei*).
△ Five Similes Elucidating the Three [Vows]: The first simile illustrates the fault of non-recollection.
For example, there is one person who is single-mindedly intent on remembering, and another who is single-mindedly intent on forgetting.

"Single-mindedly intent on remembering" means to remember the Buddha and sentient beings; it is to initiate the *saṃnāha* (vow of armor) at the very beginning of the mind and to maintain great compassion until the end.
In responding to calamities, there is none who does not keep sentient beings in mind. By what causes and conditions can they be made to escape this burning house?

If even one person is exclusively forgetful, it serves as a metaphor for the loss incurred when sentient beings fail to maintain mindfulness. The true suchness (tathatā) of the essence and characteristics of the six realms of sentient beings is equal to that of the Buddha;
yet, because they turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of sensory objects, they wander aimlessly through the six paths, lost in a profound darkness beyond investigation.
△ Second, the analogy: though encountered, it is of no benefit.

For these two kinds of people, whether they encounter [the Buddha] or not, or whether they see him or not, the Buddha and sentient beings are fundamentally inseparable; what "encountering" or "seeing" could there be? It is simply that sentient beings distance themselves from him of their own accord.
Because one person may have focused their mindfulness while another encountered or saw someone who had lost it, they neither encountered nor saw [the Buddha].
Furthermore, people today do not see the true body of the Buddha, nor do they know their own own universal essence and great function;
thus they claim that the Pure Land is a false teaching and that Amitābha is not real, speaking words that deny both the Buddha and the Pure Land.
It is like ants gathering upon a human body; they truly do not know the person. Does one become a non-person simply because of this ignorance?
Have you not heard what the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The Buddha-body fills the Dharma-realm, appearing universally before all sentient beings;
responding to conditions as they arise, its reach is never incomplete, yet it eternally remains upon this seat of Bodhi"? Alas, how can this be?
Due to the conditions of one's affinity with the Buddha, one may encounter him and yet not encounter him, or see him and yet not see him.

If one explains this through the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*), then whatever is enacted is none other than the place where the fundamental Buddha appears; all forms are the Buddha’s forms, and all sounds are the Buddha’s sounds.
Because one turns one's back on awakening and unites with the sensory dusts, one gives rise to afflictions when beholding the true realm.
To hear the wondrous sound yet give rise to distracted thoughts is truly to meet and yet not meet, to see and yet not see.

△ Third, an analogy for the attainment of mindfulness of the Buddha through mutual remembrance between two people: when their remembrance is deep in this way, it continues from birth to birth until they are as inseparable as a form and its shadow.
They do not conflict with one another.

If the first person, who is habitually forgetful, can be like the person who is habitually mindful—never failing to remember at any time or in any place—and if these two minds face one another, it may be said that their two forms of mindfulness are profound. If this is so, then in every birth they will constantly see the Buddha.
Everywhere one beholds the Tathāgata; from this moment until reaching the Pure Land, we shall be like a form and its shadow, never separated.
If the mind that contemplates is upright, the image of the Buddha remembered will appear straight before us.

Now, with single-mindedness and without forgetfulness, there shall be no encounter with the discordance of non-meeting or non-seeing. Because we now recollect one another, it is just like the inseparability of a form and its shadow.
Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of the mind: "Every thought-moment constantly accords with the fundamental principle; every mind ceases the illusory dust.
When one merely returns to the original nature, not a single dharma is newly created. Sixth, the analogy of the Dharma:
"The Tathāgatas of the ten directions pity sentient beings as a mother remembers her child. If the child has run away, though she remembers him, what can she do?"
The preceding passage regarding the two people remembering one another was a general analogy; now, when we cite the analogy of a mother remembering her child, it is most pertinent.
How much more so is the Tathāgata’s compassionate mindfulness of sentient beings, which exceeds even that of parents? Why is this?

It is because there are places where parents cannot reach with their remembrance, yet the Tathāgata remembers them; furthermore, the remembrance of a parent for a child lasts no longer than a single lifetime.

The Buddha keeps sentient beings in mind until they attain Buddhahood, at which point his mindfulness of them finally ceases. As for the "son who has run away," although it is a metaphor, it is not established in vain;

there must be a basis for it. If we discuss this in terms of causes and conditions, the "one who has run away" refers to those who, during the time of the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, entered the Mahāyāna family but subsequently regressed from the Great Vehicle in the interim—this is what constitutes having run away.

This is the time [to practice]. For one who cultivates the contemplation of the mind, if not even a single thought arises, then mother and child dwell in one place, free from the entanglements of both;
as soon as a worldly thought sprouts, it flees away into the six sense objects, becoming increasingly distant day by day with nothing to return to.
Thus, there is longing and remembrance, just as a person whose child suffers feels a particular compassion, like a mother remembering her child. This is the first point.
Question: If one is intent on remembering, yet despite remembering what is the use? For it is precisely the same person who is intent on forgetting. Question:

Since both parents possess a heart that loves their child, why does the scripture mention only the mother and not the father? Answer: Because the father’s love is strict and distant, while the mother’s love is compassionate and intimate;
therefore, the father is not mentioned. △ Seventh: Presenting the Analogy and Applying it to the Case.
If you, my son, remember your mother as she remembers you, then throughout successive lives, mother and child shall never be separated by great distance.

Although the mother’s remembrance mentioned above is earnest, if the son remains in a distant land with only idle, lingering thoughts, this is precisely what it means to "remember yet do nothing about it.
For a traveler, if one can truly remember one's mother, one must surely return to one's hometown. If a son can remember his mother as the mother remembers him, [then they shall not be parted].
What makes this especially difficult? It is that while a son may remember his mother only occasionally, a mother’s remembrance of her son is without interval.

Whether she sits upright gazing afar, forgets her meals and neglects her sleep, halts her shuttle, or ceases her weaving—there is no time when she is not remembering her son, and no place where she is not thinking of her child.
Her remembrance may truly be called profound, as if she were a mother herself.

When one is in a foreign land and yearns for one’s parents, even if that person is said to be supremely filial, or possesses excellent wisdom and a beautiful wife, or enjoys honor and wealth—such things may entangle the mind, yet they can never equal the profound longing felt when remembering one’s mother.
If this is true for the filial, how much more so for the unfilial? Therefore, the phrase "remembering as one does for one’s mother" is itself the recitation of the Buddha’s name.
This Dharma gate is most intimate; how could one allow it to pass by with negligence? When two minds face one another, how could there be any estrangement?
If one can take the heart of a parent as one’s own heart, this may be called the ultimate form of filial piety.
Throughout successive lifetimes, mother and child remain mindful of one another and do not become distant; thus they never fall into discord. This is the subsequent method.
Combined. △ Eighth, the application of the Dharma to the analogy:
"If a sentient being’s mind recollects the Buddha and thinks of the Buddha, they will certainly see the Buddha in the present or in the future.

"If a sentient being’s mind" refers to the responsive capacity that can evoke [the response]. "Recollecting the Buddha" means contemplating the Buddha who is inherently present within oneself as the subject of recollection.
Regarding the cause of being moved by mindfulness of the Buddha: that which is moved—the other Buddha—is taken as the fruit of the responsive manifestation.

This is called the perfect interfusion of cause and effect, where the principle and the phenomenon are mutually inclusive like a box and its lid; the path of resonance and response intersects, such that it is truly beyond the reach of thought or speculation.

Furthermore, "recollection" refers to the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which belongs to the internal; it is the function of recollecting the marks and signs of the True Body through diligent practice.

This refers to the way a mother remembers her child; likewise, one who recollects the Buddha (buddhānusmṛti) employs the dharma-gate of buddha-recollection to contemplate other Buddhas, encompassing both external objects and the power of wisdom.
This precisely means that throughout successive lifetimes, mother and child do not become estranged or distant.

As for "certainly seeing the Buddha in the present and the future": those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom find that everything before their eyes is nothing but the pure realm, and every step they take is [in accordance with it].
This site of enlightenment is what is called Vairocana pervading all places; is this not seeing the Buddha before one's eyes?

For those of dull faculties and shallow wisdom who, by recollecting another Buddha, gradually mature so that the nine grades of lotuses bloom in the Pure Land of the future—is this not seeing the Buddha in the future?
△ Ninth: Birth and the Buddha are not separated.
Not far from the Buddha, without relying on expedient means, one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind.
The minds of sentient beings fundamentally possess the ten dharma-realms; whenever a single thought arises, it inevitably falls into one of these realms.

If the mind recollects the Buddha and mindfulness of the Buddha is maintained, this mind is present in every moment within the Buddha-dharma realm. Although there are distinctions among the nine realms, all together constitute Buddhahood.

Are the realms not already close at hand? Furthermore, a single thought-moment is itself the fruit—the sacred name of the Buddha—since it does not rely on the fifty-five stages of expedient means within the causal path;
therefore, it is said that "expedient means are not required. After a long time, it is spontaneously realized, like awakening from a great dream or the blooming of a lotus flower;
thus, it is said that "one spontaneously attains the opening of the mind. However, some people seek other expedient means elsewhere.
"Is it appropriate to practice mindfulness of the Buddha only after the mind has been opened and the intellect liberated? He replied: "One need not rely on other expedient means;
the spontaneous opening of the mind itself is sufficient proof that this single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha is already the most supreme expedient, requiring no others.
Furthermore, while each of the twenty-four sages relied on different expedients, they all ultimately reached the perfect function through the faculties of hearing, reflection, and cultivation."
This single gateway of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) is so exceedingly easy that it may cause people to become suspicious and turn back.
You must therefore hold fast and believe with certainty. Whether you achieve success or not, whether you reach the Pure Land or not, in all your actions, take the Buddha as your mindfulness.
If even a single thought of delusion arises, this is precisely where your mindfulness of the Buddha is lacking. Thus it is said.
If you contemplate and visualize for a long time, your mind will open of its own accord; provided you have the resolute mind, you will certainly not be deceived.
△ The Ten Similes: Without relying on expedient means, it is like a person who has been smeared with incense, whose body acquires a fragrant scent; this is called "Adornment of Fragrant Light."

Just as when people are anointed with incense, they immediately acquire its fragrance which permeates their bodies—this serves as a direct analogy for how by being anointed with mindfulness of the Buddha, one attains Buddhahood.
What skillful means could there be that would allow sentient beings to borrow [the Buddha's qualities] if they do not practice mindfulness?
It is clear that if they do practice mindfulness, the wondrous fragrance of merit will permeate their minds. As for "adorned with fragrant light," this refers to the Buddha who is the teacher.

Since he is named "Immeasurable Light," how could he not possess "Immeasurable Fragrance"? Furthermore, when one recollects the Buddha and the Buddha is recollected, the Buddha resides within the practitioner’s conduct, mind, and speech;
how could this be anything other than adornment by fragrance and light? △ Eleven: Conclusion on Self-Benefit.
"In my original ground, I entered the patience of non-arising through the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha."

As for the mind of mindfulness of the Buddha (*nienfo*), one maintains the three contemplations (*sanguan*) and the Buddha possesses the three bodies (*sanshen*). By destroying the three delusions (*sanhe*), if one contemplates through the gate of emptiness (*kongguan*), one contemplates the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) Buddha;
entering the two patiences of acquiescence (*fushun erren*), one destroys the delusions of views and thought (*jiansihe*) and accomplishes the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*).

If one contemplates through the gate of the provisional (*jiaguan*), one contemplates the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) Buddha; entering the patience of non-arising (*wushengren*), one destroys the delusions of the sands of the Ganges (*chenshahe*) and accomplishes the virtue of liberation (*jietuo*). This is the middle contemplation (*zhongguan*).
Recalling the Dharma-body Buddha, one enters the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa-kṣānti*), destroys ignorance and delusion, and accomplishes the virtues of the Dharma-body.

Here, speaking in terms of the causal stage, the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) should be understood as occurring within the stage of partial truth (*bhūta-tathatā-vibhāga*).

From the section on the "Instruction in the Buddha-remembrance Samādhi" up to the "Adornment of Fragrant Light," the conferred Dharma-gate is described; it is only here that [the author] personally recounts his own original cause. Do not [omit this].
Not entering the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti) by means of recollecting the Buddha or mindfulness of the Buddha is self-benefit within this causal stage.
△ Twelfth, after realization, transforming others:
now, within this world-system, he gathers those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha and returns them to the Pure Land.
This proves that after his own self-benefit, he also benefits others; for since he has benefited himself by this means, he likewise uses it to transform others.
If there are those in this realm with the capacity for mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), he will surely gather them in and lead them to the Pure Land, thereby fulfilling his original vow.

△ Thirteenth: Mañjuśrī answers the Buddha’s question regarding perfect penetration. "I have no preference; I simply gather the six sense-faculties together, maintaining pure mindfulness in succession, thereby entering samādhi—this is the foremost."
The World-Honored One commanded the twenty-five sages to each describe their realization of perfect penetration. The Sutra states: "I now ask you:

regarding your initial aspiration for enlightenment, among the eighteen realms, which did you take as the path of perfect penetration? By what skillful means did you enter samādhi, and by what sequence have you reached this point?

This refers specifically to the cultivation of the sense-base of sight (*cakṣur-āyatana*) within the section on the seven elements. As for the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), it belongs to the sense-base of mind (*mano-āyatana*) and is therefore secondary.
"Controlling all the faculties" means that for one whose mind is fixed on the Buddha, the eyes observe while the mind remains present;
by turning the gaze back and withdrawing the hearing, when one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation.
"Pure mindfulness succeeding one another" means that the mind focused on the Buddha must not, for even a single moment, dwell on the five worldly desires; such a single thought constitutes purity.
To begin with, the state of uninterrupted moment-to-moment continuity is difficult to clarify; therefore, I shall provide a further illustration by means of a metaphor.
In the Western Heavens (India), there is a precious gem called the "Pure Pearl. Why is it named the Pure Pearl?
If this pearl is cast into turbid water, for every inch it enters the water, it produces one inch of clear water—whether it be two inches, or even up to a foot or a fathom.

Reaching the bottom of the abyss in succession until nothing remains that is not pure is a perfect metaphor for casting the pure pearl of mindfulness of the Buddha into the turbid water of the deluded thoughts of sentient beings;
the water of deluded thoughts cannot but become clear.
Thus, when people today recite the Buddha’s name even once, it is like the pearl entering the water: for every inch it travels, one inch of clarity is attained.
When the mind shifts its attention to the second sound, it is like a pearl entering water: at two inches, one obtains two inches of clear water;
and so on, up to ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand, a million, and even to the immeasurable.

Just as a pearl sinking deeper and deeper can cause the bottom of the water to become completely transparent, so too, when the thought-pearl is cast into turbid water, that turbid water cannot but become clear. This is the power of mindfulness.
The Buddha casts himself into chaotic thoughts so that chaotic thoughts may not fail to be eliminated; this can be called "pure mindfulness succeeding one another.
*Samādhi* is simply an alternative designation for *samāpatti*. The preceding [discussion on] the patience of non-arising was realized through *samādhi*;

that [passage] cited the object manifested to reveal the subject, whereas here the subject is cited to reveal the object. This mutual citation of subject and object is a refinement of literary expression. Thus it is.
Regarding "being foremost," this refers to the Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha through the Power of Avalokiteśvara being foremost.

In cultivation, one must first ensure that one's footing is firm; do not act with the instability of an ordinary person (*mārga*), which is like a rat gnawing at a granary—by gnawing from a single spot, there will naturally be a point of entry. If, however, one gnaws here and there...
Even if one were to gnaw on a donkey’s hoof for years, there would be no point of breakthrough.

An ancient master said, "If you wish to practice the direct path, it lies solely in single-mindedly reciting the Buddha's name. This is the essential maxim of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*).
The Commentary on the Section on the Perfect Penetration of Mahāsthāmaprāpta (End)
